items.prompt: Which of these is a sponsor?
choices: Someone who speaks up for you in a meeting you skip
Someone who gives you tips over coffee when you ask them
Someone who reads your draft and sends private feedback
items.explanation: A sponsor advocates where you cannot be present.

items.prompt: What does a mentor mainly give you?
choices: Public advocacy in meetings you are absent from
A share of their own reputation as cover for you
Private advice, usually when you ask for it
items.explanation: Mentors advise; the advice stays in the conversation.

items.prompt: Where does a sponsor's support take place?
choices: Only in private one-on-one talks with you
In rooms you are not part of
Only in written feedback sent to you directly
items.explanation: Sponsorship happens where you have no voice.

items.prompt: What does speaking up for you cost a sponsor?
choices: Some of their own standing if they are wrong
Only a few minutes of their time that day
Nothing, since the advocacy is on your behalf
items.explanation: They put part of their reputation behind yours.

items.prompt: Marcus's friendly colleagues all agree the reorg looks wrong. What did they do for him?
choices: They protected him by agreeing with him in private
They acted as sponsors by sharing his concern
Nothing that reached the director, since none spoke
items.explanation: Private agreement never leaves the lunch table.

items.prompt: Which one protects against decisions made about you without your input?
choices: A mentor who gave you good advice last month
A sponsor present in the decision room
A friend who agrees with your view privately
items.explanation: Only someone in the room can influence the decision.

items.prompt: Which pair is described correctly?
choices: Mentor advises you; sponsor advocates for you
Mentor advocates for you; sponsor advises you
Mentor and sponsor both act mainly in private
items.explanation: The roles differ in what they do and where.

items.prompt: Priya's senior colleague raised her work with the director unprompted. What role was he playing?
choices: Mentor, because he cared how her career went
Friend, because he knew her well enough to help
Sponsor, as he spent his own credibility on her
items.explanation: Unprompted advocacy in her absence is sponsorship.

items.prompt: A coworker says in a 1:1, 'I'd tell your director the reorg is unfair, if I were you.' Two days later the director presents the reorg without them saying anything. Which description fits that coworker?
choices: A sponsor: they gave a clear opinion about the situation
A mentor: the advice reached you but never reached the room
A bystander: they offered nothing helpful about the situation
A critic: they judged the director's decision to be unfair
items.explanation: The advice was good, but sponsorship means acting in the room, which this coworker never did.
items.reference:
Mentor vs. sponsor
mentor: advises you, in private, when asked
sponsor: speaks for you, in rooms you are not in
cost to a sponsor: part of their own reputation
Why: advice only works when you are in the room; advocacy works when you are not.
items.learnMore:
Where support happens

The two roles differ by location and cost, not by quality of advice. A sponsor takes your case into rooms where you have no voice and spends their own credibility doing it.

Common mistake

Counting a friendly colleague who agrees with you in private as protection against decisions made in a room you are not in.
items.reflection: Think of someone at work who has advised you well. Has anyone ever spoken for you in a room you were not in, and how would you have known?

Only the second gives advice that is likely to be accurate
Only the first is likely to spend any personal credibility
Only the first can help the engineer with later career choices
items.explanation: Advocacy in absence is the protection; accuracy of advice and warmth are not what separate them.

Only after an unfair event has occurred
Well before any trouble starts

A sustained pattern of useful, reliable work
A list of compliments you have given leaders
items.explanation: It is built from many occasions, not one.

choices: About 67%
About 6%
About 100%
items.explanation: The model gives roughly 67% at month 24.

items.prompt: According to the model, how do the odds change from 6 to 12 months?

They stay at exactly zero
They rise, but remain low

Careful, useful work done repeatedly near a leader

It takes up a lot of their calendar time
It requires them to know your whole career story

Like an ordinary day of routine teamwork
Like the need-timed move it is

items.prompt: Is the model curve a measurement of real people?

No, it is a simple teaching model
Yes, it is an average from many companies
items.explanation: It illustrates a shape, not data.

items.prompt: On the unit's modeled curve, an engineer has 6 months of genuine track record and a crisis arrives. Which statement fits?
choices: Odds are already high, since the work was genuinely done
Odds of unprompted advocacy are still low, around 6%
Odds are exactly even, since six months is a half year
Odds depend only on how senior the colleague is
items.explanation: The curve is flat early; six months of work is still near the bottom.
items.reference:
Modeled advocacy odds
month 6: about 6%
month 12: about 19%
month 18: about 40%
month 24: about 67%
Why: teaching curve, not a measurement: slow at first, steep later, so a crisis-time burst sits at the bottom.
items.learnMore:
Why trust cannot be rushed

A sponsor needs evidence from many occasions, gathered without pressure to be impressed. Goodwill is banked early and spent late, and the biggest withdrawal needs the deepest history.

Common mistake

Treating sponsorship as something you can request in a crisis, instead of something that has to already exist.

items.prompt: What separates genuine coalition-building from manipulation?
choices: Whether you planned it in advance
Whether the usefulness is real
Whether the person is senior or not
items.explanation: Planning is fine; fakeness is the problem.

items.prompt: Which counts as genuine?
choices: Careful useful work that is visible
Flattery aimed at someone with influence
Helping only when the leader is watching
items.explanation: Real work is real regardless of the audience.

items.prompt: Which is transactional manipulation?
choices: Doing careful reviews for a colleague's design doc
Crediting the right team after a shared incident
Performing friendliness only for their influence
items.explanation: Performance without substance is the problem.

items.prompt: What happens to a performed relationship under scrutiny?
choices: It tends to grow stronger
It tends to collapse
It tends to stay unchanged
items.explanation: It has nothing real to stand on.

items.prompt: If a senior person never sponsors you, was genuine effort wasted?
choices: No, you still did good work and built a tie
Yes, the only goal was getting sponsorship
Yes, the work was pointless without a payoff
items.explanation: Genuine effort has value regardless.

items.prompt: What is the anyway test?
choices: Would your manager approve of the act?
Would the senior person notice it quickly?
Would you do it if they had no influence?
items.explanation: It checks whether the help is real.

items.prompt: Does planning to build useful relationships make them manipulative?
choices: Yes, any planning counts as manipulation
No, the deliberate part is not the problem
Yes, unless you tell people your plan first
items.explanation: Intent to be useful is not the issue.

items.prompt: Why does flattery fail as sponsorship material?
choices: It is not evidence a sponsor can trust
It takes too long to write and deliver well
Senior people dislike all kinds of praise
items.explanation: Sponsors act on evidence, not on compliments.

items.prompt: Two engineers each spend a month helping a director's team. One would have done it for any team; the other does it only because the director controls promotions. Which relationship is likelier to hold when tested?
choices: The second, because more deliberate effort was invested
The first, because that help was real regardless
Neither, since helping a director always looks staged
Both equally, since the work done was the same
items.explanation: The test is whether the help would exist anyway, not how much effort went in.
items.reference:
The anyway test
would you do it if they had no influence?
yes: genuine, and it holds up under scrutiny
no: performed, and it fails when scrutiny arrives
Why: being deliberate is fine; the usefulness has to be real.
items.learnMore:
Deliberate is not the same as manipulative

Planning to build useful relationships is fine. What matters is whether the help is real and whether it would exist even if the relationship never paid off.

Common mistake

Assuming any intention to build alliances is manipulation, or assuming flattery counts as usefulness.
items.reflection: Recall a time you helped someone partly hoping it would pay off. Would you have done it anyway, and how did they respond?

Could the idea help her chances this week?

Her recent two years of work
The platform group
items.explanation: She did not tie the idea to the decision.

Doing a normal review as usual that same day

items.explanation: Manufactured usefulness is the problem.

items.prompt: After raising the idea, what did Priya do about the decision?
choices: Nothing beyond a normal week
Asked Tomas how the choice was going
Dropped hints about wanting a place
items.explanation: She did not steer toward it.

items.prompt: Why does Priya treat not knowing the effect as fine?
choices: She forgot to follow up on the decision
She was sure the idea hurt her chances
The aim was never to engineer a result
items.explanation: Genuine acts are not tied to outcomes.

items.prompt: Priya learns a decision about her is coming and also has an overdue useful idea. Which approach follows the unit's reasoning?
choices: Hold the idea back so the timing does not look suspicious
Raise the idea as usual, without mentioning the decision
Raise the idea and mention the decision to explain the timing
Add extra help this week to show how reliable she is
items.explanation: The anyway test says do what she would have done; hiding or leveraging both distort it.
items.reference:
Priya's motive check
idea: raise the retry-logic fix, planned for weeks
question: would I do this without the decision?
answer: yes, so raise it, and mention nothing else
Why: timing can be coincidental; the act is genuine if it would have happened anyway.
items.learnMore:
Checking your own motive

When convenient timing appears, the question is not whether it could help you but whether you would have acted anyway and whether you shaped the act around the outcome.

Common mistake

Inventing a reason to be useful because of an upcoming decision, or steering a conversation toward it.

Adapting the case

Priya had two years and a person whose word carried weight. If either differs, the aim stays the same, which is credible evidence in front of someone with standing, while the route and the timeline change.

Common mistake

Copying Priya's two years as a fixed schedule, or assuming sponsorship needs personal closeness.
items.reflection: In your current setting, who has standing and the chance to see your work? What small, real thing could you do this month that you would do anyway?

items.prompt: Which change to Priya's story would most affect how fast the approach works?
choices: Using a different programming language on the project
Having a different name for the ledger service
Having far less than two years before the trouble starts
Meeting at a different time of day on the same team
items.explanation: The timeline changes what is possible; the rest is incidental.
items.reference:
When the details change
new to the org: month one of the clock starts now
difficult senior person: evidence beats warmth
partial substitutes: mentor plus a documented record
Why: the timeline is a shape, not a script; sponsorship needs credible evidence, not years or friendship.
